encounters.cc: Persistent thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue

lines: Persistent thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue

The patient is a 16-year-old male with Kallmann syndrome, Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, and traumatic central diabetes insipidus who presents to the emergency department six months following a prior admission for diabetic ketoacidosis.
He was in his usual state of health until 4 days ago, when he began experiencing persistent thirst and frequent urination.
He initially attributed it to hot weather and increased physical activity but became progressively fatigued.
His parents brought him to the emergency department when he began vomiting repeatedly and complained of diffuse abdominal pain.
On the morning of admission, he appeared drowsy and was breathing heavily and rapidly.
He denies recent illness, medications, or toxin ingestion.

On physical examination, he appears ill, with sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, and deep, labored Kussmaul respirations.
He is oriented only to person.
Capillary refill is delayed.
There are no focal neurologic deficits, but he is slow to respond and appears confused.
Cardiac and pulmonary exams are otherwise normal.
Initial labs reveal a serum glucose of 620 mg/dL, pH of 6.98, bicarbonate of 6 mEq/L, serum sodium of 131 mEq/L, serum potassium of 5.1 mEq/L, and positive serum ketones.
Serum creatinine is mildly elevated, and the calculated anion gap is 24.
He is started on IV fluids and an insulin infusion, with telemetry monitoring and close electrolyte follow-up.
Over the next several hours, as his glucose levels decline and acidosis begins to resolve, his serum potassium drops rapidly, requiring additional potassium chloride infusions.

encounters.cc: Worsening epigastric pain and vomiting 2 days after MVA

lines: Worsening epigastric pain and vomiting 2 days after MVA

The patient is an 18-year-old male with Kallmann syndrome, Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, and traumatic central diabetes insipidus status post recent motor vehicle collision, who returns to the emergency department two days following the initial trauma with worsening abdominal complaints.
He was involved in the collision two days ago, where he sustained a seatbelt injury to his abdomen.
He was initially discharged after a brief observation period with no significant findings on the abdominal examination.
However, he now reports severe, constant pain in the epigastric region that worsens with movement.
He has vomited multiple times, with the vomitus initially containing food particles and now being bilious.
He denies any hematemesis, melena, or bowel movement since the accident.
